The brake temperatures eventually began to rise and the Fire/Rescue lead could see some smoke and at some point said possibly a flame, they sprayed water on wheel truck. This produced immediate results and temperatures were lowered and no further visible smoke or fire evidence. I did not feel evacuation was necessary and the Fire/Rescue lead agreed with that judgment as well as Copilot's. At some point Fire/Rescue advised the number 2 tire had deflated as a protection. Maintenance Control and ZZZZ Operations were all utilized. With the brake temperatures now at normal readings and in coordination with Fire Rescue and Operations the passengers were briefed on deplaning with airstairs onto buses and brought to terminal. Eventually the entire [crew] left the plane onto a bus. Operations/maintenance lead confirmed the aircraft would be towed for inspections.
ASRSN:1916526.s: The flight crew rejected takeoff on Runway XXR due to a persistent R HYD QTY EICAS caution message. Fire/Rescue personnel extinguished smoke from overheating brakes and a deflated tire, allowing passengers to deplane safely while the aircraft was towed for inspection.

ASRSN:1916558.n: At about 2,000 feet AGL on final for ZZZ Runway XXR, flaps 20, PF (Pilot Flying) calls for gear down. Within about 30 seconds after EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System) reports Gear Disagree and Nose Wheel Door Open Warning Messages. We executed a go-around, and during the go-around procedure the warnings disappear. PF calls for the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook), and we complied with the QRH to the full extent that we could. Since all indications were normal and we had three green down and locked indications we decided not to request priority handling. We were vectored around and had a normal, uneventful landing and taxi in. We had been flying Aircraft X the entire day, and we as a crew both noticed that the gear retraction/extension transition times were unusually longer than we were used to. On climb out from ZZZ1 back to ZZZ we were already through 1,000 feet AGL before the gear was fully up. We sent an ACARS message to dispatch as a heads up.
ASRSN:1916558.s: The crew of Aircraft X experienced delayed gear retraction and false EICAS warnings on final approach, prompting a go-around. After warnings cleared and three green indications confirmed, they completed a normal landing without requesting priority handling.

ASRSN:1916560.n: L Bleed Duct Warning. Bleed Valves closed. [Requested priority handling]. Returned to ZZZ no incident.Repair bleed valve duct.
ASRSN:1916560.s: The crew experienced an L Bleed Duct Warning and closed bleed valves, requesting priority handling to return to ZZZ. No incident occurred, and the bleed valve duct was subsequently repaired.

ASRSN:1916561.n: Closed Crew Door prior to takeoff, Door Warning Light extinguished. On takeoff heard whooshing noise and noticed (rear) bayonet on crew door was not engaged. Returned and landed uneventfully. Inspecting the door after the event, the crew door trailing edge sticks out 1' from the airplane frame even though the front of the door was properly seated. The crew door was twisted out at the aft of the door and unusual closing force was needed to pull in the trailing edge.
ASRSN:1916561.s: The flight crew reported a crew door bayonet failure during takeoff, where the door appeared latched but twisted open at the trailing edge. The aircraft returned and landed safely after the crew noticed the misalignment and unusual closing force required to secure the door.

ASRSN:1916568.n: On initial climb out, we got a 'HYD Y ENG 2 PUMP LO PR' ECAM message. No quick action or ECAM exception, so we followed the ECAM actions. This directed us to turn off the yellow hydraulic pump, which caused the PTU to take over the yellow system. We then read through the follow up items in the QRH, and started to make a plan. The Captain gave me the aircraft and proceeded to contact Dispatch and Maintenance for their opinion on the situation. It was concluded that we would return to ZZZ, and I then began coordinating the return to the field. Since we would be an overweight landing, we [requested priority handling] and received priority handling to the runway of our choice with emergency vehicles standing by. We requested that Approach Control vector us around in a box pattern over the airfield while we ran all the appropriate checklist and made all the appropriate communications/preparations. Once everything was complete, and we were comfortable to commence the approach, the Captain flew the ILS/Visual to XXR for a landing well within overweight tolerances. Once clear of the runway, we had the emergency equipment check us over for hot brakes or any other visible issues, and requested they follow us to the gate. We then taxied back to the gate and deplaned. On climb out , ECAM HYD Y ENG 2 Pump LO PR. ECAM action preformed as ECAM. QRH follow up and status page reviewed. Returned to ZZZ to do a non normal overweight landing. All checklist procedures where accomplished while receiving ATC vectors as a [priority] flight. We landed safely with no damage to aircraft.
ASRSN:1916568.s: The flight crew received a HYD Y ENG 2 PUMP LO PR ECAM message on initial climb, followed procedures, and returned to ZZZ for an overweight landing. They received priority handling and ATC vectors to complete checklists, landing safely with no aircraft damage.

ASRSN:1916577.n: Approximately 15 minutes after departure, Green Hydraulic Overheat was annunciated via ECAM. Procedures followed, with system pump placed to off. Follow-up procedures also completed. First Officer and I discussed best course of action. A declaration of emergency to ATC was not warranted given the abnormal condition, in our opinion. Pan-Pan-Pan was offered to ATC, requesting a change in routing, keeping us closer to suitable diversion airport should further issue(s) develop. This request was honored. Overheat condition abated approximately 30 minutes into the flight. To allow for additional cooling, engine driven pump was not reactivated until near ZZZ1. Monitoring the hydraulic page of ECAM, system pressure returned to normal, overheat did not reappear and flight continued for normal landing ZZZ. Dispatch informed me of one, or more, events of same issue has occurred. Dispatch was utilized to relay updates between flight, maintenance and ZZZ, including possible need for stop on runway and towing to gate. Once system remained in normal condition, Dispatch et al was informed, as was ATC, a normal landing was expected.
ASRSN:1916577.s: The flight crew experienced a Green Hydraulic Overheat 15 minutes after departure, placing the system pump off and requesting a Pan-Pan routing change to stay near a diversion airport. The overheat abated, the pump was reactivated near ZZZ1, and the aircraft completed a normal landing at ZZZ.

ASRSN:1916584.n: While operating ZZZ-ZZZ1, we sustained a Smoke, Odor, Fume event shortly after take-off resulting in a return and landing at ZZZ. I was acting as the Pilot Flying on this flight. Pre-flight, gate departure and taxi out were all normal with no anomalies. Departing Runway XX, the take-off roll, rotation and initial climb out were uneventful. At approximately 600-800 ft. AGL, after gear retraction but prior to any flap retraction, the flight deck phone chimed from the cabin. The Pilot Monitoring answered the call to hear FA (Flight Attendant) number four reporting smoke in the aft cabin that was increasing and causing his eyes to water and throat to burn. The FA was notified that we would return to ZZZ and asked to report any changes to the situation. The CA (Captain), Pilot Monitoring, advised me of the situation and of our need to return to ZZZ. At that time [we requested priority handling] with the Tower Controller who acknowledged the [priority] and handed us off to Departure. During this phase of flight the Pilot Monitoring communicated with the cabin crew and the passengers of our need to return to ZZZ for a precautionary landing. I communicated with ATC and flew the aircraft on vectors around to Runway XY. The Pilot Monitoring executed the QRC checklist for Smoke Odor Fumes and continued into the QRH to the extent time allowed. The same was accomplished with the Overweight Landing procedure. I landed the aircraft on Runway XY in a Flaps 30 Autobrakes 3 configuration with a normal touchdown and rollout. We exited the runway where we were met by and immediately put in contact with ARFF (Airport Rescue and Firefighting) Personnel. They did a visual inspection along with temperature readings and reported no anomalies. The cabin crew reported the dissipation of smoke at that time as well. In coordination with ARFF they escorted us to [Spot] XX where they asked us to have passengers remain seated while they boarded the aircraft for an inspection. After doing so, they reported it was safe to deboard the aircraft which occurred normally. Maintenance took the aircraft from that point after AML entries were made by the CA. We received a new aircraft, reboarded and flew the original ZZZ-ZZZ1 trip with no abnormalities. In light of the unknown source of the smoke, emphasis was placed on returning to ZZZ in an expeditious but safe manner over completing all QRH items for [the] event. Nothing to suggest.
ASRSN:1916584.s: The Pilot Flying and cabin crew of ZZZ-ZZZ1 experienced increasing smoke in the aft cabin at 600-800 ft AGL shortly after take-off, causing a return to ZZZ. The aircraft landed safely on Runway XY with no anomalies found by ARFF, and the trip was completed on a replacement aircraft.

ASRSN:1916590.n: After deadheading into ZZZ I arrived at Gate XX where passenger boarding had already started. I had pulled up the release ahead of time (while the deadhead flight taxied in) and had noticed 3 MELs (including the APU and the APU bleed) and 1 CDL on the release. When I arrived at the cockpit I observed that the APU was already running. I questioned the Mechanic who was there at the time working on a #2 RMP write up and she knew nothing about it. The ground power AVAIL light was not illuminated and the APU bleed was off. I called Operations to request that the Ground Crew check the GPU connection and the ground power switch. We were unable to get ground power established so I requested a ground power cart. Operations replied that they would try and find one and that it 'could be awhile.' I reviewed the maintenance logbook and noted that the APU was definitely still on MEL status and was on the Logbook Deferral sheet. I also noticed that the aircraft had experienced a fume event the day prior. I called ZZZ Maintenance and Disptach to advise them of this. While on the phone with Dispatch, ground power was established and I switched over to it and shut the APU down. While talking with Dispatch, a ramp person disconnected the ground air without any notification to us and the temperature rapidly rose to 92 degrees in the cabin. I went outside and questioned why this was done. No answer was available. I requested HP air be connected so we could more efficiently cool the cabin. Ground Personnel did this and I proceeded back to the cockpit, Shortly after running HP air through the packs, we detected a chemical smell in the aircraft and I turned off the packs, The Mechanic onboard smelled it too and requested the packs be turned back on so that she could verify it and see if the Flight Attendants noticed it as well. Citing crew and passenger safety, I refused. I left the cockpit to ask the Ground Crew to reattach low pressure ground air. I noticed two men in sport coats at this point in the jetway. They later introduced themselves as ZZZ Chief Pilots and graciously offered any assistance necessary. I called Dispatch to inform them of the situation and request that the Equipment Coordinator find a new aircraft. The LP ground air was once again disconnected for some unknown reason and the cabin climbed to 96 degrees. I made the decision to deplane the passengers at this point and coordinated with the Gate agent. As we were deplaning, a ZZZ Chief Pilot informed me that he had contacted the last crew and they had used the APU on both legs because Maintenance had told them it was okay to do so.Cause - The previous crew's decision to use the APU, despite it being on MEL.1. Thoroughly investigate Smoke/Odor/Fume events before the aircraft is released back into service. It is an extremely serious safety concern and I do not feel like it is treated this way based on my experience. 2. As has been requested by crews many times, have Ramp Personnel request the removal of ground air just like the procedure to remove electrical power. Ground crews should not arbitrarily remove this without any notification to the flight deck!
ASRSN:1916590.s: The pilot reported that the previous crew operated the APU despite it being on the MEL, causing a fume event and cabin overheating when ground air was disconnected without notice. This led to passenger deplaning and a request for a new aircraft due to the chemical smell and safety concerns.

ASRSN:1916600.n: Cabin Altitude warning on descent. The cabin altitude was over 10,000 feet. We donned our oxygen masks, requested priority handling, and descended to 10,000. We ran the checklist during the descent. We continued the flight from there without further incident. The Captain did a great job coordinating everything once we got the warning. Cause was aircraft system malfunction. On descent at 22,000 feet we had a Cabin Altitude Warning. The cabin altitude had climbed to over 10,000 feet. Ran the checklist, requested priority handling in order to get priority for a rapid descent to 10,000. Rest of the flight was uneventful. Great job by First Officer.
ASRSN:1916600.s: The flight crew experienced a cabin altitude warning exceeding 10,000 feet during descent at 22,000 feet due to an aircraft system malfunction. They donned oxygen masks, requested priority handling, and descended to 10,000 feet, completing the flight without further incident.

ASRSN:1916620.n: Filed late due to access not being active. While climbing through FL270 we received a R BLEED DUCT Warning. The Pilot Flying leveled off around FL270 and the Pilot Monitoring began running the QRH (Quick Reference Handbook). Both bleed valves closed and the Pilot Flying began a descent to 10,000 feet IAW (In Accordance With) with the QRH and ECS (Environmental Control System) configuration. Advised ATC that we needed to descend to 10,000 feet immediately. They initially authorized descent to FL240. We again advised it had to be 10,000 feet. They authorized FL180. At that time, we [requested priority handling] and descended to 10,000 feet. The Pilot Monitoring completed the QRH procedure, after working with Dispatch and Maintenance Control, the flight continued to ZZZ unpressurized without further incident. Mechanical issues occurred on subsequent flight on Date.
ASRSN:1916620.s: The crew encountered an R BLEED DUCT warning while climbing through FL270, causing both bleed valves to close. They descended to 10,000 feet after requesting priority from ATC and continued unpressurized to ZZZ following QRH procedures.

ASRSN:1916633.n: Aircraft X landed earlier in the day at ZZZ with a maintenance issue. Talking with the Captain from that flight, he told me they had a L PACK TEMP EICAS Message with a PACK OFF and INOP overhead lights. They could not reset the pack using the QRH procedure, so [they] turned it off. He then said the cockpit started getting very hot. They couldn't control the temperature and it became so hot they eventually had to descend below 10,000 feet, depressurize and turn off the Right Pack.When we arrived at the airplane, maintenance was deferring the Left Pack. I asked about the temperature problem with the right that the previous crew had inbound. Maintenance informed us that they had tested the Right Pack and it checked normal. We started the APU and ran the Right Pack. Air was very cool and seemed to be working normally. After engine start and during taxi/take off/initial climb out, the pack still worked normally. When the flaps were retracted and the pack went to Hi-Flow, the air seemed to get warmer but not bad. By 10,000 feet the flight deck temperature was approaching 30 degrees. We continued the climb but eventually asked ZZZ Center if we could stop at FL260 while we worked an A/C temp control problem. By then the flight deck temp was up to 39 and slowly climbing. We tried turning the Flight Deck Auto trim switch to manual and holding it in the cold position. The trim air needle moved toward the cold position, but it just kept getting hotter.We turned the right pack control switch to N, but it got hotter. We turned off the trim air switch, still got hotter. By now we determined there was no way we could continue to ZZZ1, as flight deck temp was now 45. First Officer flew the airplane and took left comm (ATC communications) while I attempted to contact Flight Control/Maintenance on AIRINC. Phone patch finally went through but it was hard to communicate as the reception was bad. I was able to notify them of the problem and said we could not continue to ZZZ1 but needed to land somewhere else. We mutually decided ZZZ2 (by this time we were approaching ZZZ3). I felt ZZZ2 was a good choice. Flight Control ran the numbers for us and gave us weather and NOTAMs. I asked if we could get Name on the phone and informed him that there was a possibility of an overweight landing. Between Name, Maintenance and I, we determined the best plan was to go straight to ZZZ2 and land (overweight if necessary). The First Officer coordinated with ZZZ2 Center for a reroute to ZZZ2. We began our route and started to descend for 2 reasons:1. It was now 47 degrees C in the flight deck (117 F) and we needed to get below 10,000 feet so the Right Pack could be shut off.2. I wanted to get down and burn off more fuel to hopefully get below 43,000 pounds wing fuel and 283,000 pound landing weight.We went down to 8,000 feet, depressurized and shut off the right pack. We also extended the spoilers in an attempt to burn more fuel. By the time we passed landmark we were down at 4,000 feet, flaps 5, 200 knots with spoilers extended. This all worked out as fuel on board was 43,000 lbs and aircraft weight was 282500. We were handed off to ZZZ2 approach and asked for vectors to [Runway] XX final for the visual. We retracted the spoilers and completed the approach and landing normally.Of note, as we were descending, both Captain and First Officers iPads overheated and shut down. This was unexpected and not something I had been thinking about. I got out of the seat and put both in the catering cooler for about five minutes. Fortunately this worked and they both turned back on.
ASRSN:1916633.s: The crew of Aircraft X experienced uncontrollable flight deck heating due to a Right Pack failure during climb, forcing a diversion to ZZZ2. They descended below 10,000 feet to depressurize and shut off the pack, burned fuel to reduce landing weight, and successfully landed after cooling overheated iPads in a catering cooler.

ASRSN:1916638.n: The event occurred while taxiing on the ZZZ ramp around D concourse. We were cleared by the east ramp frequency to taxi from our present position (pushed back off or EX) to spot 24X and contact the south ramp frequency. Immediately after receiving our clearance, an Aircraft X was cleared to make a right turn to spot 25X and contact Ground. Approximately a minute later, while rounding the corner from the north to south west, near spot 26 we had noted that there was an Aircraft Y that was stationary off to our right, further down the D concourse near gates D3 or D5. Shortly after passing spot 26 the Aircraft X turned out and proceeded immediately in front of us with no apparent regard for our direction of movement. Our Captain had to aggressively brake to ensure we would avoid the aircraft. Throughout this whole time, there was no communication from either the Aircraft Y, or the Ramp Controllers on involving any potential traffic conflicts on the ramp or having either us, or the Aircraft Y stop to avoid the conflict.
ASRSN:1916638.s: While taxiing on the ZZZ ramp, our aircraft was forced to brake aggressively to avoid Aircraft X, which turned in front of us near spot 26. The reporter attributed the conflict to a lack of communication from Ramp Controllers regarding traffic between our aircraft and stationary Aircraft Y.

ASRSN:1916666.n: I arrived on shift on Date at XA PM for our unscheduled engine change on Aircraft X. after clocking in, I walked to the airplane to verify documentation had been generated and what all was left to accomplish prior to hanging the new engine on the aircraft [had been complied with]. I noticed that there was not a single non routine created to address the forward mount. Given that we consistently have issues with damage being found on the FWD engine mount, I went to look and found a large gouge on the FWD alignment pin hole. This item had been documented previously in Year under item XXXXXXX ref EAXXXXXXa. After reading through the documentation, I noticed a discrepancy with the reported information under the EA and the condition on the aircraft and generated item XXXXXXY for the new damage. The previous EAXXXXXXa does not reference the harsh edge left in the guide pin hole. Original documented damage was .150 into the hole, .080, and .335 around the circumference of the hole. The current conditions of the damage are .168 into the hole, .090 wide, and a circumferential length of .225 with a hole size of .858. Per SRM XX-XX-XX-XXX-XXX figure 5, a 40:1 blend ratio of the width of damage is required to be accomplished, and as such should have originally been documented as 3.2' long around the circumference of the hole. The total hole circumference is only 2.7' around. In order to remove a 40:1 blend out with the current dimensions, you would need a 3.7 inch circumferential chamfer.Additionally, there is cross section removal limit of .0039. the reported cross sectional removal limit was .006, and currently sits at .00756. This damage is out of limits per SRM and DOES NOT MATCH the data reported in the initial EA. The current damage as shown on the aircraft, the items with arrows are in limits per SRM, but have not been added to any EA technical document.Due to management pressures and consistent request for rushed engine changes, things can be missed. We are consistently being asked to overlook and reassess all the time. Given all the eyes on our station for engine changes (Aircraft X having an aborted takeoff on #2 engine after #1 engine change, Aircraft Y needing a fuel pump/HMU after lockup during start, and Aircraft Z requiring extensive fitting rework due to LESS damage than reported here, why we can allow this to go as 'previously reported damage' without the EA containing any mention of sharp edges left in the fitting hole is beyond me. Reduce management pressure on Technicians to ensure a safe and quality product is provided to our customers. People fly on our planes, and it is our job to correct any unsafe condition to the best of our ability. Reduce the number of unqualified mechanics working engine changes in our high stress environment. This is not a job that can be done by someone who has not had the experience of doing them. They will continue to misinterpret, miss document, and incorrectly perform maintenance when there is not someone there to guide them.
ASRSN:1916666.s: A mechanic discovered undocumented gouge damage on Aircraft X's forward engine mount during an unscheduled engine change, noting the condition exceeded Structural Repair Manual limits and contradicted previous records. The reporter attributed the oversight to management pressure for rushed maintenance and the presence of unqualified technicians in a high-stress environment.

ASRSN:1916698.n: Crew detected hissing sound and attempted to identify source. In the process of scanning cockpit and instruments we noticed the differential pressure was abnormal for the altitude and immediately donned oxygen mask and started priority descent to 10,000 feet and requested priority handling with ATC. Our destination was about 50 minutes and fuel remaining would not be sufficient for flight at ten thousand feet to our destination. So we decided to divert to ZZZ. Cabin Altitude Light came on during descent and went out at ten thousand feet. We landed uneventfully on Runway XXL.
ASRSN:1916698.s: The flight crew detected a hissing sound and abnormal differential pressure, prompting an immediate priority descent to 10,000 feet and a diversion to ZZZ due to insufficient fuel for the destination. The cabin altitude light illuminated during descent but extinguished at 10,000 feet, and the aircraft landed uneventfully on Runway XXL.

ASRSN:1916731.n: During departure from ZZZ the ALT1 warning light came on. Cycling the ALT1 power did not clear the warning. I requested a return to ZZZ where a complete shutdown and restart also did not clear the warning light.A local Mechanic, familiar with the SR22, identified the problem as a failed ALT1 and he did not have the capability to repair the part that day.We discussed the possibility of returning to the home airport ZZZ1;70 nM away, in VFR conditions. [The Cirrus SR22 ALT2/BAT2 system is made to operate the ESSENTIAL buss (which includes the PFD and GPS1) continuously and is completely isolated from ALT1 (engine instruments are then displayed on the PFD)]. The circuit breakers for the MFD and GPS2 could be pulled to reduce the electrical load on BAT1, saving its capacity in the event it should be needed to take over from the ALT2/BAT2 system if it were to fail.This was discussed (by phone) with a second Mechanic that normally maintains the airplane and he agreed that this process would work. The POH was not reviewed.After landing, the POH was reviewed, and it was determined that ALT1 is required equipment for all flights.TAKEAWAY -- The POH governs, not the hopes of the PIC (Pilot in Command) or statements by Mechanics.
ASRSN:1916731.s: The pilot of a Cirrus SR22 experienced an inoperative ALT1 warning during departure from ZZZ and returned after mechanics confirmed the failure. Although mechanics suggested continuing to ZZZ1 by isolating systems, the pilot later determined the flight was invalid because the POH requires ALT1 for all operations.

ASRSN:1916732.n: Upon boarding I noticed a rancid/locker room smell that continued throughout the cabin. I asked the other Flight Attendants and they said they did not smell anything. When we were descending the odor got worse and the #2 Flight Attendant said she smelled what seemed to her to be burning plastic smell. The smell did not change for me only got worse upon descent.
ASRSN:1916732.s: A Flight Attendant reported a rancid odor in the cabin that worsened during descent, while another crew member detected a burning plastic smell. The reporter noted the odor persisted throughout the flight and intensified as the aircraft descended.

ASRSN:1916741.n: Training in progress. Trainee released 2 C208 aircraft off of ZZZ1 airport. These aircraft are assigned 255 heading and 4000 ft. altitude. Trainee then released a C510 off of ZZZ2 airport on 260 heading to 4000 ft. I thought the trainee was going to climb the C510 above the 2 departures then turn north. He ended up changing his plan at the last second and climbing the first C208 to 6000 ft. and stopping the second at 3000 ft. Once the C510 got to 4000 ft. he turned it northbound. This had him heading for a 6000 ft. MVA. The trainee ended up getting distracted by other aircraft and wasn't climbing the C510. I instructed the trainee to climb the C510. He still wasn't climbing fast enough so I told him to turn it west away from the MVA. The trainee gave him a heading westbound but it still did not end up being enough and the aircraft entered the 6000 ft. MVA below 6000 ft. I should have stepped in earlier and over keyed the trainee. This particular trainee has a lot of experience so I chose to tell them what to do instead of keying the frequency myself but that ended up being the wrong decision. I also found out later that the trainee was having severe back pain and ended up going home sick.
ASRSN:1916741.s: An instructor and trainee controller managed departures from ZZZ1 and ZZZ2, where a C510 entered a 6000 ft MVA due to delayed climbing and insufficient westward turns. The incident resulted from the instructor's decision to verbally instruct rather than override the controls, compounded by the trainee's distraction and severe back pain.

ASRSN:1916742.n: While working R35 I observed the traffic building and several red numbers approaching on the TSD (Traffic Situational Display) board for R52. Weather was building and at least 2 large MOAs were active. All of our sectors were already split as much as possible. I notified Controller in Charge (CIC) of the problem and the CIC notified Traffic Management Unit (TMU) immediately. Front Line Manager (FLM) relieved CIC for break shortly after. It seemed that nothing had been done to alleviate the approaching red blocks. I notified FLM about the situation and asked if he had already done everything possible to slow the traffic down. I volunteered to call W35 and W09, since R52 was already getting busy, and have them route a few aircraft west over the coastline. FLM said 'it was fine'. I told him it was about to get bad and this was our only chance to fix it. He said 'turn around and face my scope'.I was surprised at the apathy but I did as told. I don't know if any further action was taken. I was relived for break shortly thereafter and briefed my relief that R52 was about to be very busy and to help however possible. I remarked to R51 that I was surprised nothing was being done. He wasn't surprised and said that the same thing happened yesterday. When I returned from break R52 with a Dside was completely down the toilet with traffic, weather, and JAINS deviations. The TSD was showing 4 blocks of solid red and the rest yellow with numbers from 28-35. The maximum for R52 is 23 under ideal conditions. I couldn't count all the aircraft but I would estimate that he had nearly 40 on his scope at one point. Most were deviating and asking for different altitudes. Half of his transmissions were 'standby, or unable requests'. A tracker was paged back from break. It took over an hour to stabilize the sector. R35 also noted what a mess it was.I've seen plenty of sectors get too busy or unsafe in my career. This was, however, the most easily preventable situation I've seen. R47/48 were combined the entire time because they were slow. 5-10 aircraft could've been routed through their space every half hour and would have been easily managed. I'm not sure if TMU took any action but it certainly wasn't enough. I was willing to call W35/W09 and ask them to climb anyone capable up to R51 and to route a few specific planes around R52 to prevent this. I was basically told to mind my own business and not to worry about it.
ASRSN:1916742.s: An R35 controller reported that R52 became overwhelmed with traffic, weather, and JAINS deviations due to insufficient mitigation by the Front Line Manager and Traffic Management Unit. The sector exceeded capacity with nearly 40 aircraft, requiring over an hour to stabilize after the controller's proposal to reroute traffic was rejected.

ASRSN:1916748.n: I was working as Controller in Charge (CIC) observing both Local and Ground Control, as well as dealing with administrative duties. The Local Controller had successive, same fix departures and he informed me that he was vectoring the second departure to gain required lateral separation. He asked that I inform the Departure Controller that he was doing so, but did not tell me nor did I hear what heading he issued to Aircraft X. It became apparent shortly thereafter that the Controller had issued a heading that put the aircraft into an MVA around an obstruction. The Departure Controller then called back on the shout line instructing the Local Controller to turn the aircraft immediately away from the obstruction. By this time the Local Controller had already issued and the aircraft was in a turn away from the obstruction. After being made aware of the proximity to the obstruction and reviewing the event, the vector issued was drastic, and a less divergent heading should have been issued.
ASRSN:1916748.s: The Local Controller issued a drastic vector to Aircraft X for lateral separation, placing it at risk of Minimum Vectoring Altitude violation near an obstruction. The Departure Controller intervened to order an immediate turn away, which the aircraft executed after the Local Controller had already initiated the maneuver.

ASRSN:1916830.n: Took off behind a B767 and after clean up, think we hit his wake turbulence as the jet rolled hard left. Simultaneously we heard a bang and received a warning of an engine stall with the right engine rolling back. As soon as the FO (First Officer) called out 'my aircraft' the engine recovered and went back to climb power and the ECAM message went away. All engine parameters were normal so we continued to ZZZ1. Not sure what caused the stall, but the right engine started very slowly and the FO and I both commented that we might have a hung start. The engine did finally get up to speed without any ECAM messages and was within normal parameters. Did happen to notice after the stall occurred and was closely monitoring that engine that the fuel flow was about 200 lbs/hr higher than the left engine and the EGT was about 40 degrees higher.Maybe wake turbulence or maybe a bad engine. Not sure what Maintenance found.
ASRSN:1916830.s: The crew experienced a right engine stall and wake turbulence roll shortly after takeoff behind a B767. The engine recovered automatically, but the pilot noted higher fuel flow and EGT, suspecting either wake turbulence or a hung start.

ASRSN:1916831.n: During Maintenance Ferry Flight of a long-term storage, Block I aircraft, from ZZZ to ZZZ1, the crew experienced abnormal/erratic airspeed and altitude indications on the Integrated Standby Flight Display (ISFD) passing approximately 15,000 ft. The Flight Crew elected to perform immediate action items and referenced the QRC and QRH. We requested to level off and a turn back towards ZZZ while coordinating holding in order to accomplish QRH procedures. Following QRH procedures we determined that both CA's (Captain) and FO's (First Officer) airspeed were reliable and isolated the problem to the ISFD using ground speed, true airspeed, AOA and related power setting and pitch attitude for the airspeed being flow. Crew elected to [request priority handling] and requested vectors to the RNAV (GPS) Runway XX at ZZZ. An uneventful land was made at ZZZ.Equipment malfunction.None. The ISFD was found to have malfunction and was removed and replaced.
ASRSN:1916831.s: During a maintenance ferry flight of a Block I aircraft, the crew encountered erratic airspeed and altitude indications on the Integrated Standby Flight Display (ISFD) near 15,000 ft. After isolating the fault to the ISFD and verifying primary instruments, they returned to ZZZ for an uneventful landing and subsequent equipment replacement.

ASRSN:1916835.n: Approaching final approach fix for Runway XXR with a configuration of gear down and flaps 20, asked for flaps 25. First Officer put the flap handle to 25 and shortly after we received a 'Trailing Edge Flaps Disagree' EICAS (Engine Indicating and Crew Alerting System) and Discreet Light. The flap position indicator showed approx flaps 24. Executed a go-around as commanded by the First Officer. Performed QRH (Quick Reference Handbook) procedures and requested priority handling. Landed uneventfully on Runway XY. Cause was flap system failure. Aircraft had a flap disagreement and went around and landed on Runway XX. Radio chatter between the crew and ATC made me aware that they in fact were a 'priority aircraft'. Crew did request priority handling as a precaution. Aircraft landed and blocked in without another incident. The rest of the radio chatter between ATC and the crew was about securing the priority.
ASRSN:1916835.s: The crew experienced a trailing edge flap disagreement and EICAS warning while approaching Runway XXR with flaps 20, prompting a go-around. They executed QRH procedures, requested priority handling, and landed uneventfully on Runway XY due to a flap system failure.

ASRSN:1916850.n: Aircraft was at gate and was just finishing up the boarding process. The door had just been closed when a vehicle struck aircraft. Initial indication felt like tug had just connected tow bar with a slight jar. Captain was notified by ground personnel that a vehicle had just struck the right side of aircraft just below the APU exhaust. Maintenance was notified that aircraft had been struck by vehicle and evaluated damage. It was determined that damage was beyond flyable limits. Crew notified appropriated personnel and deplaned the aircraft. Aircraft was turned over to Maintenance. Maintenance was notified and determined that there was damage to aircraft.
ASRSN:1916850.s: While the aircraft was at the gate finishing boarding, a ground vehicle struck the right side below the APU exhaust. Maintenance determined the damage exceeded flyable limits, resulting in the crew deplaning passengers and turning the aircraft over for repairs.

ASRSN:1916861.n: After parking on spot 1 and when we were in the midst of our shut down flows, the parking brake released. I had my feet on the brakes on the rudder pedals, but apparently not enough as the aircraft rolled a couple of inches. In fact, when it happened, I thought to myself, 'Good thing I have my feet on the brakes.', and wasn't aware we had rolled at all until my First Officer asked, 'Are we rolling?' By the time she asked, the aircraft had stopped and she noticed her brakes were ineffective as my feet were still holding pressure on the brakes.
ASRSN:1916861.s: During shutdown flows after parking on spot 1, the parking brake released and the aircraft rolled a few inches while the Captain held the rudder pedals. The First Officer noticed the movement and found her brakes ineffective because the Captain's feet were still applying pressure.

ASRSN:1916875.n: On takeoff after positive rate we selected gear up. During the gear up cycle we had a landing gear disagree issue and could not get the right main wheel up. Once we ran the checklist we put the gear down and [requested priority handling]. We made a return to airport with a low approach to check the gear down position. Cause was there was an issue with the weight on wheels sensor.
ASRSN:1916875.s: The flight crew experienced a landing gear disagree issue on takeoff where the right main wheel failed to retract due to a faulty weight-on-wheels sensor. They executed the checklist, returned to the airport for a low approach to verify gear position, and requested priority handling.

ASRSN:1916881.n: Taxiing into Gate. Marshalers getting ready. Started turn to align aircraft with gate line but not enter gate area. Turn would encroach on vehicle roadway in front of gate area. Cleared left and cleared right. In turn, FO called out to stop. A fuel truck ignored aircraft movement and marshalers and continued at high speed in front of our aircraft. I was forced to slam on breaks to avoid a collision. Another aircraft reported a similar incident moments before our incident. Same fuel truck. I contacted operations and advised of the incident. The other aircraft also contacted operations to advise of their incident.
ASRSN:1916881.s: During taxiing to the gate, the flight crew stopped the aircraft to avoid a collision when a fuel truck ignored marshals and crossed the path at high speed. The pilot reported that the same truck had caused a similar incident with another aircraft moments earlier.

ASRSN:1916884.n: I was returning from the lav during cruise. The FO (First Officer) said the EICAS decluttered as soon as the FA (Flight Attendant) was leaving the flight deck so I could return. The indication was high vibrations in the Low Pressure Stage of Engine 2 that read 4.0 in yellow. We were at FL330 and M0.78. I sourced the aircraft to my side. We ran the QRH. We descended and slowed down as recommended. Each time we were able to establish a vibration reading in the green it was a power setting unable to maintain airspeed per the QRH and even with asymmetrical thrust. I believe we descended and slowed the aircraft down 2 additional times than what the QRH recommended and finally at FL270 and unable to hold 230 KIAS to maintain a normal vibration indication I decided to proceed with the engine shutdown procedure and land as soon as possible. I would request more clarity be added to the QRH while running the Engine Abnormal Vibrations QRH checklist.
ASRSN:1916884.s: During cruise at FL330, the crew encountered high vibrations in Engine 2's Low Pressure Stage. After descending and slowing beyond QRH recommendations to FL270 without resolving the issue, the Captain shut down the engine and diverted to land as soon as possible.

ASRSN:1916886.n: Everything from the moment we got into the aircraft at the gate, and all the way up until just after the top of climb was normal. Everything was operating normally, some MELs, but we already knew about it. The Captain went to the lav, and the Flight Attendant took the open seat according to the Company's procedures. I showed her how far we had to go and how much time we have left on the PROG page on my FMS, then I noticed an amber indication off the left corner of my eye. I noticed the LP vibrations on the right engine was 4.0 amber. All other vibrations were no higher than 0.5 and green. The entire EICAS was full. Once the Captain returned I immediately showed him. He pulled out the QRH and we ran the Engine Abnormal Vibration checklist. QRH called to slow down .02 mach, so we did. Went from .78 to .76. No change, it went to green for a few seconds, but came back to amber. It also called to descend 2000 ft., so we did. Went from FL330 to FL310. No change, it went to green for a few seconds, but came back to amber.Then we tried again going down to FL290 and slowed our airspeed. Again, no change, it went to green for a few seconds, but came back to amber. I cannot recall if we tried a third time, I think we did, but I do remember being at FL270. We tried reducing the power on the affected engine to maintain green LP vibrations and (if I recall) increasing the non affected engine. But we weren't able to maintain airspeed. I believe at this time we were around 230 kts. and decreasing. Up until this time, I was PF (Pilot Flying). CA (Captain) decided its safer to secure the affected engine and divert. I agreed. I believe we agreed upon a diversion airport before we shut the engine down. I thought ZZZ was a good option. It was one of our bases, also one of our maintenance bases too. It was ~180nm away. CA thought ZZZ1 was a better option since it was closer (~120nm). We then both agreed on ZZZ1. We checked the weather at ZZZ1 and it showed VFR. CA requested priority handling and we got vectored to ZZZ1. At this point we switched roles. I became PM (Pilot Monitoring) and he became PF. We did hand over the controls multiple times to assist each other in other tasks throughout the diversion/descent. Basically, anytime I was reading the checklist, I was PM. Anytime CA was making a call to the passengers and FAs (Flight Attendant) in the cabin, I would be PF. Right after CA [advised] ATC and got a vector to ZZZ1, we secured the affected engine. Next, I could not recall which order these were in, but we accomplished these tasks in the order of the QRH: I got our landing speeds from the shutdown checklist. CA notified Dispatch via ACARS. CA notified FAs. CA notified passengers. I had difficulty clearing out the flight plan by dragging the destination airport to the top. CA helped, but had difficulty too. It could be a bug in the planes computer, it's an older E170. I just deleted every fix by hand. It only took about 20 seconds.Multiple descent clearances and headings. Visual app and landing XXL.
ASRSN:1916886.s: The First Officer and Captain experienced high right engine LP vibrations at FL330, prompting a descent and speed reduction that failed to resolve the issue. They secured the engine, diverted to ZZZ1, and landed safely after switching roles and manually clearing the flight plan due to FMS difficulties.

ASRSN:1916892.n: We were on final cleared to land XXR back into ZZZ. There was an Aircraft X that just touched down Runway YY. Their instructions were cleared to land, they decided to do a touch and go without proper authorization and rotated directly into us. At the time of their rotation, we were just about to cross over Runway YY. ATC told Aircraft X to turn immediately left heading 230. We immediately turned right and climbed as traffic was turning directly in front of us. They received a possible pilot deviation and we safely entered a right downwind YY and landed. At the closest point we were within 500 ft. of their aircraft.
ASRSN:1916892.s: While on final for Runway XXR, the crew encountered an unauthorized touch-and-go by Aircraft X on Runway YY, which rotated directly into their path. The crew executed an immediate right turn and climb, maintaining a 500-foot separation before safely landing after Aircraft X received a pilot deviation.

ASRSN:1916898.n: Pressurization issue. Once we reached 10,000 feet, a huge whistling noise went throughout the cabin. When I went to call The Captain, she called me and informed me that we were returning to ZZZ. I prepared the cabin and treated the situation as priority. I gave everyone their duties. When CA informed me about anything, I informed the PAX (Passengers). Masks did not deploy. No one needed medical attention. No damage was done on the inside of cabin nor from what I can see from exit windows. Passengers and UMs were reassigned to gate for next flight. I remained calm for Passengers and did as I was trained and told by CA. CA and FO was very good at helping handle the situation. I was able to continue working the next flight to ZZZ1. Another FA said she reported this same issue, same plane on Date. Come to find out there was a leak coming from cockpit window left side.
ASRSN:1916898.s: Cabin crew reported a pressurization issue with a loud whistling noise at 10,000 feet, prompting a return to ZZZ. The cause was identified as a leak from the left cockpit window; masks did not deploy, no injuries occurred, and passengers were reassigned.

ASRSN:1916925.n: I was coming in to land and ballooned slightly. The nose was pointing slightly left when it settled back down. The airplane ran off the left runway. I was unable to steer back to the center line of the runway. Student freaks out being by himself on solo. Did prior landing/takeoff training, and performed just fine. Landed and just ran off the runway.
ASRSN:1916925.s: A student pilot soloing a landing ballooned slightly, settled with the nose left, and ran off the left side of the runway. The pilot could not steer back to the centerline, attributing the incident to the student panicking despite prior successful training.

ASRSN:1916951.n: Left Engine failed to produce power 15 minutes out from finial destination ZZZ. Feathered left engine, requested priority handling and flew straight in approach RNAV XX to ZZZ field without issue. Inspection of aircraft found fuel leaking from left engine main fuel tank filler cap. Inspection of filler cap showed cap chain pinched between fuel cap and body of filler neck breaking the seal and allowing fuel to be siphoned from tank in flight. Fuel bladder was also found to be lifted up due to vacuum of fuel being siphoned and caused fuel gauges to read full when in fact the tank was empty. Per installed instruments, more than 2 hours of fuel should have been left in the aircraft however the left main was emptied due to imperfect seal on left main tank filler cap.
ASRSN:1916951.s: The pilot reported a left engine power failure 15 minutes from destination ZZZ due to fuel siphoning caused by a pinched filler cap chain breaking the seal. This vacuum lifted the fuel bladder, causing gauges to falsely indicate full tanks while the left main tank emptied, forcing a priority RNAV approach.

ASRSN:1916958.n: I was in a climb about 10 miles north of ZZZ to 11,500 as the air was cold and my C172 was climbing well when I felt like a sudden loss of engine power. The RPMS kept dropping and rising as I pumped the throttle. I immediately felt like I was losing my engine and requested priority handling with ATC. They started vectoring me towards the airport for an immediate landing. After about 3-4 minutes ATC suggested I pull the carburetor heat, which fixed the issue. I did have to keep the carb heat in for 6-7 minutes to fully melt the carb ice in the carb. Once I felt the situation was back under control I canceled the request for priority handling and continued to my destination at 9,500 feet back to ZZZ1.
ASRSN:1916958.s: A C172 pilot experienced sudden engine power loss and RPM fluctuations during a climb to 11,500 feet north of ZZZ, prompting a priority landing request. ATC advised applying carburetor heat, which resolved the carb ice issue, allowing the pilot to cancel priority handling and continue to ZZZ1 at 9,500 feet.

ASRSN:1916969.n: Pilot involved was scheduled to meet CFII for biannual flight review/training. After pre-flight as per the checklist, there were three attempts made to start the aircraft for warm up purpose only. The battery was low and the starter unable to move the propeller through the first compression stroke. At that time the only occupant of the aircraft exited without properly completing the shut down checklist with the intent of pulling the propeller through the first compression stoke by hand. As a result of not following the shutdown checklist the Master switch was turned off, the mixture left full rich, and the magnetos in the both on position. When the propeller was pulled through the first compression stroke the engine started with no occupant in the aircraft to shut down the engine.
ASRSN:1916969.s: A pilot attempting to hand-turn the propeller on an unoccupied aircraft after a failed start caused the engine to run away. The incident occurred because the pilot skipped the shutdown checklist, leaving the master switch off, mixture full rich, and magnetos on.

ASRSN:1916972.n: Taxiing from the Ramp near Taxiway at ZZZ, Ground Control gave instruction to taxi to Cargo ramp via Taxiways X, and Y, clear to cross Runway XX/XY, and hold short of Runway XZ/XA. Following the assigned route, barrier was encountered across Taxiway after crossing Runway XX/XY. The barrier was not noticeable in the dark due to low reflectivity until the aircraft was right at the barrier and there was not sufficient time to stop. Fortunately the barrier was small and there was no damage to the aircraft from crossing over it. I informed the Ground Controller of the barriers and he commented he was under the impression the barriers had been removed and apologized for the situation.
ASRSN:1916972.s: The pilot encountered a low-reflectivity barrier on Taxiway Y at night while taxiing to the Cargo ramp at ZZZ. The aircraft crossed the barrier without damage, and Ground Control apologized, stating they believed the barriers had been removed.

ASRSN:1916980.n: While operating as a crew-member of a UAS flight, the pilot ground station indicted battery level of 49% and the remaining time in excess of 10 minutes. While operating at a distance of 150 meters or less, this did not create a concern over low fuel. About a minute after the check at those numbers, the aircraft went into return to home mode due to a very low fuel condition (20%). Pilots elected to not delay the maneuver and allowed the aircraft to land automatically to prevent an in-flight fuel exhaustion. During the return to home maneuver the aircraft passed over a previously densely occupied lawn that may have been considered flight over people as some people were still on the lawn.
ASRSN:1916980.s: A UAS pilot experienced an unexpected drop from 49% to 20% battery, triggering an automatic return-to-home landing to prevent fuel exhaustion. The aircraft subsequently flew over a previously occupied lawn where people were still present.

ASRSN:1916994.n: Aircraft X, on final for Runway 28L, transmitted a question about Aircraft Y, turning to final for Runway 28R, their flight path, and intentions. Aircraft X then came back and said they were responding to a TCAS RA and going around. We (myself and Local Control (LC)) notified the Controller in Charge (CIC) of the TCAS RA, noting that we agreed Aircraft X concern, that we both observed that Aircraft Y appeared to cross through centerline, it was likely significant and possibly a NMAC, and that we were going to Brasher Aircraft Y. After landing, Aircraft Y was given the Brasher and Ground Control (GC) provided them with the Tower phone number. Upon review by the staff specialist there was no issue or loss and when the pilot called the Tower, they stated that they did not cross centerline, and the CIC said that they did nothing wrong. Upon my review, maximum separation at one point was .12 laterally and 200 ft. vertically, with the aircraft at one point being within 100 ft. vertically. Furthermore, the replay with centerlines depicted, clearly shows Aircraft Y flying through centerline and despite the radar replay not having centerlines, and also depicts it. Had Aircraft X not responded so quickly, the two aircraft would have been significantly closer, especially considering the already close proximity of the finals. In the essence of safety, this issue should not have been brushed off so easily by the staff specialist, nor the CIC. And despite, the CIC's unnecessary comments, saying something and giving the Aircraft Y pilots the Brasher is not to 'take away some pilot's license', but instead to highlight a potentially significant issue and error on the part of a pilot's actions. Safety is always the first priority and making it seem as though the mistake is insignificant leads us down a slippery slope.
ASRSN:1916994.s: Aircraft X executed a TCAS RA go-around on final for Runway 28L due to Aircraft Y crossing the centerline while turning to final for Runway 28R. The reporter observed minimum separation of 0.12 NM laterally and 100 ft vertically, criticizing the subsequent dismissal of the potential NMAC by the Controller in Charge and staff specialist.

ASRSN:1917001.n: Aircraft X checked on level at 060 was issued a climb to 070, however did not read back. Attempted standby radios, guard frequency, and other aircraft (high alt, and low alt.) to reach the aircraft. Neither myself or Washington Center could reach the aircraft. The aircraft entered a 061 MVA NORDO. The best solution to this problem would be to get better radios.
ASRSN:1917001.s: Aircraft X failed to read back a climb clearance to 070 while level at 060, resulting in a loss of radio contact with Washington Center. The aircraft subsequently entered a 061 MVA NORDO, which the reporter attributed to poor radio equipment.

ASRSN:1917002.n: Traffic was busy, sector was red on the NAS monitor. Numerous aircraft were climbing and descending and needed reroutes. Neither I nor the D-side noticed that Aircraft X was filed SABAT-QUERY at 130. He started flashing as he was several miles into the 133 terminal airspace. By the time I realized what was happening and that he wasn't on a transition route he was descending out of 135. I attempted to stop him at 133 but he descended down to 127 before he could correct. He subsequently climbed back to 133 and was cleared for the approach from QUERY. The controller I relieved said he received Aircraft X descending to 130 from sector 08 and didn't notice the error. The sector 08 controller said that Aircraft X was originally filed SABAT-WYS where 130 was a good altitude but he requested SABAT-QUERY and she was extremely busy without a D-side and not catch the error. Double check MVAs whenever an aircraft below 160 requests a route change. Hire enough staffing to have D-sides and split sectors where necessary. Aircraft X was issued a pilot discretion descent to 130 which would keep the aircraft above terrain but then requested a change in routing over QUERY which is in the next sector, Sector 06. I gave Aircraft X their requested routing of SABAT direct QUERY but was so busy I didn't think to check the MIA in sector 6's airspace, if I had I would have stopped the aircraft at 140. I was inundated with deviations, sequencing for Denver and had so many aircraft and no D-side. Request more staffing so that we can split sectors when needed and/or staff d sides.
ASRSN:1917002.s: An air traffic controller issued Aircraft X a route change to SABAT-QUERY without verifying the Minimum IFR Altitude, causing the aircraft to descend to 127 instead of the filed 130. The controller attributed the error to high traffic volume, lack of a D-side, and failure to check terrain constraints during the busy sector.

ASRSN:1917014.n: I cleared Aircraft X for an ILS Approach at WYS initialing over SABAT. The transition in not a straight-in transition. The published altitude after SABAT on the transition is 11,500. After I changed Aircraft X over to advisory frequency, they proceeded to descend to 10,000 after SABAT, 1,500 feet below the published altitude, then intercepted the localizer and skipped the procedure turn altogether.The ILS Approach at WYS needs an IAF that allows for a straight-in (noPT) approach. The current ILS Approach is grossly inefficient and is incorrectly flown by airline on a regular basis. While descending to 10,000 on the SABAT transition is still at my MIA, the pilot has no altitude guidance below those altitudes published on the approach. I have reported this in the past. At the time (pre-COVID) there were communications taking place to add a fix (perhaps FEVIP) to create a straight-in option. Pilots were also briefed that they were flying the approach illegally. It appears we are back to square one with no changes made to the ILS Approach and pilots flying it incorrectly.
ASRSN:1917014.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X for an ILS approach at WYS via SABAT, but the pilot descended to 10,000 feet, 1,500 feet below the published 11,500-foot altitude, and skipped the procedure turn. The controller attributes this incorrect operation to an inefficient approach design lacking a straight-in option, noting pilots have been warned they are flying it illegally.

ASRSN:1917024.n: Santa Fe Tower called for a release on Aircraft X northbound on the POAKE2 departure procedure. They told me to 'keep an eye on him because he doesn't seem very bright'. He was released and departed a few minutes later off Runway 2. It became clear that the pilot was not flying the departure procedure and more looked to be flying runway heading into high terrain NE bound. He entered a 110 MIA block below 100 and a low altitude alert was issued and he was advised it didn't look like he was flying the departure procedure. He then corrected his routing to re-join. It seems to be a more common issue than not that aircraft depart SAF either misunderstood to fly present heading or not knowing how to read the departure chart. Because of our high terrain near SAF this often results in terrain violations and low altitude alerts because we are not able to vector the IFR aircraft below terrain.
ASRSN:1917024.s: Air Traffic Controllers reported that a pilot departing Santa Fe on the POAKE2 procedure flew runway heading into high terrain instead of following the chart. This caused a low altitude alert below 10,000 feet, attributed to the pilot's misunderstanding of the departure instructions.

ASRSN:1917093.n: Dispatching out flight XXXX asked pilots to 'set brakes' and was given the response 'brakes set, cleared to disconnect'. Signaled to my wingwalker that the brakes were set and cleared to disconnect. Aircraft started rolling towards us and i had to use hand signals to get the pilots to set brakes. I reconnected headset to confirm brakes set. Pilot verbally confirmed brakes were now set again.
ASRSN:1917093.s: During pushback, the wingwalker signaled that brakes were set, but the aircraft rolled toward the crew, requiring hand signals to stop it. The pilot verbally confirmed brakes were set again after the wingwalker reconnected the headset.

ASRSN:1917095.n: Ramp loaded mail listed on guidance sheet that had incorrect weight listed. Notified Ops and Load Planning after flight took-off.
ASRSN:1917095.s: The crew discovered ramp-loaded mail had an incorrect weight on the guidance sheet and notified Operations and Load Planning after take-off. The report does not specify the aircraft type, flight phase details, or the outcome of the notification.

ASRSN:1917126.n: Cruise flight at FL360, about XA25 EDT, ZZZ1 to ZZZ2, we experienced a left engine failure. I was the Pilot Flying and the First Officer (FO) was the Pilot Monitoring. We heard a light 'bang' noise, followed by instrument indications of a left engine failure and slight to no airframe vibrations. We requested priority handling with ATC, discussed best airfield to divert to (we chose ZZZ3, about 50-60 NM away), and started receiving vectors and altitude changes for the descent to ZZZ3. The FO flew the aircraft and talked on the radio while I ran the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH) checklists for an engine failure. After all checklists were complete, I took the controls and performed a single engine landing to a full stop on Runway XXC at ZZZ3. The CFR personnel/equipment inspected the aircraft and stated all looked good. We then taxied to gate B14. Flight was cruising at FL360. We had chosen to fly west of some weather that was along the east coast. As we were just passing the ZZZ4 state line, talking to ZZZ Center, we heard a thud type noise from the left side of the plane. The engine instruments for the left engine started to show that the engine was failing. Shortly thereafter the plane yawed due to the engine failure. The Captain, who was pilot flying, immediately said 'My aircraft' and I replied 'your aircraft'. The autothrottles and autopilot were disconnected and the Captain initiated a descent while I requested priority handling with ZZZ Center. We had both agreed that from our current position that diverting to ZZZ3 would be best so I then told ATC our intentions of diverting there. I reached for the Quick Reference Checklist (QRC) to start a checklist as we were descending while getting altitudes and vectors from ATC got us headed towards ZZZ3. The QRC didn't have engine failure checklist so I went to the Quick Reference Handbook (QRH). As I got into section 7 of the QRH I asked the Captain if he'd like to run the procedure for engine failure. He then gave a positive exchange of controls to me saying 'your aircraft' and I replied 'my aircraft'. I kept the aircraft descending while the Captain ran the QRH. We continued to receive vectors and altitudes from ATC getting us into position for an approach into ZZZ3. As we approached ~13000 feet the Captain had finished all QRH driven items and checklists so I then positive exchange of controls back to him. At this point we were getting vectors and altitudes from ZZZ3 Approach and was expecting the ILS to XXC. As the Captain flew I/we briefed the approach and talked about once we got on the ground coming to a full stop and extending the flaps all the way from 15 to 40 as a precaution. We also discussed the overweight landing and what needed to be done in regard to that. We continued to descend until we were cleared for the ILS XXC approach. As we were intercepting the localizer I ran the descent checklist and before landing checklist to the line. We captured the glide slope and continued to configure the aircraft for a single engine approach while finishing the before landing checklist. The approach went smoothly and so was the landing. Once on the ground we came to a full stop. The Captain set the parking brake, I set the flaps to 40 and he got the spoilers/boards. We had the fire trucks do an inspection of the aircraft and once cleared we were able to taxi to the gate under our own power. Once safely at the gate we ran the shutdown checklist with no further issues.
ASRSN:1917126.s: During cruise at FL360, the crew experienced a left engine failure indicated by a noise and instrument anomalies, causing a yaw. They diverted to ZZZ3, executed single-engine checklists, and performed a full-stop landing on Runway XXC after a fire inspection cleared the aircraft.

ASRSN:1917127.n: Departed ZZZ, Aircraft X, to ZZZ1 on Date. Approximately 100 E/NE ZZZ2 while at FL340 at XA50Z, while deviating north for weather, the flight crew received a Master Caution and ECAM for HYD SYS LO PRSR for the Yellow Hydraulic System. Subsequently, a FLT CNTRL ECAM was received due a partial spoiler deployment (#4) on the right wing. The First Officer was the Pilot Flying and the Captain was the Pilot Monitoring. All QRC, ECAM, QRH and follow-up procedures were completed by the Pilot Monitoring. While the Pilot Flying continued the weather deviation, the Pilot Monitoring conferred with dispatch on flight options and diversion details, to include the NOTAMs for ZZZ2. A request for priority handling was made and a diversion to ZZZ2 with ATC priority radar vectors for descent. Coordination via a precautionary landing brief to the flight attendants and passenger PA were also completed. Additional information regarding the partial spoiler deployment was obtained via communication between the Pilot Monitoring and the number one Flight Attendant via a visual inspection of the right wing. There was a noticeable right wing dip at altitude and increased buffet and droop during the descent and approach phase of flight. The Pilot Flying executed a visual approach, with the electronic means of backup using the ILS XXR to an underweight landing (132,000 pounds). After clearing the Runway, an Airport Rescue and Firefighting vision inspection was executed, with the crew confirming flight crew suspicions of hydraulic fluid loss along the belly of the aircraft. With the Green, Blue hydraulic systems intact, the aircraft was taxied to Gate XX. Cause was determined to be the mechanical failure of Yellow System Reservoir. ECAM status page mentions approach phase procedures which result in return of HYD SYS LO PRSR ECAM warning (engine pump on) which can confuse with electric pump on since both work with Yellow System.
ASRSN:1917127.s: The flight crew of Aircraft X diverted to ZZZ2 after a Yellow Hydraulic System reservoir failure at FL340 caused low pressure and partial spoiler deployment. The crew executed an underweight visual approach with increased buffet, confirmed hydraulic fluid loss post-landing, and taxied to the gate with Green and Blue systems intact.

ASRSN:1917128.n: While in east hardstand after landing bleed was selected as pneumatic source before shutting down right engine. Shortly after selecting APU a crayon smell was noticed by me and I selected Auxiliary Power Unit off. We taxied to gate and shut down engine shortly before arriving at gate and deselected bleed and didn't notice the smell. Upon deplaning a deadheading Captain said he and his First Officer smelled dirty socks. We had shut down APU by then and were using ground air and power. Maintenance showed up and smelled the crayon smell and confirmed mid cabin dirty socks smell. The mechanic did a visual exterior inspection and notified me that oil was leaking from rear APU. Dispatch notified, report sent, cabin discrepancy form given to mechanic and we left with no affects or injuries. Great source of reliable information from the deadheading crew alerted me to a more serious issue than maybe what could have been construed as just crayon smell and maybe what I thought exterior smell from maybe hot brakes or otherwise. We gave APU well beyond 3 minutes before selecting bleed on.Suggestion: more awareness to speak up when a smell is not normal in cabin. Flight Attendant's in rear didn't smell anything or in the front but glad deadheading crew was able to articulate smell from their past experience.
ASRSN:1917128.s: The pilot detected a crayon smell after selecting the APU as a bleed source post-landing, while deadheading crew later reported a dirty sock odor. Maintenance confirmed an oil leak from the rear APU, resulting in no injuries or operational impact.

ASRSN:1917229.n: During the initial climbout of OKC we got an Air/Ground message on EICAS. We continued our climb and once we were out of sterile and at a safe altitude we ran the QRH, which said that we could possibly not have steering and thrust reversers. We patched through to Dispatch who connected us to a Maintenance Supervisor. The Supervisor informed us that the light would most likely extinguish when we dropped the gear. We continued the flight and decided we would compute the numbers for both scenarios, the light extinguishing, and the light not extinguishing with the unfactored landing distance times 1.7. Working as a crew we decided we would extend the gear early and that if the light did not extinguish we would request priority handling out of an abundance of caution and in case we didn't have reversers or steering.When we got the ATIS at ZZZ they were using the east directional runways and the winds were out of the South, 20 gusting 30. According to the QRH we were supposed to run the unfactored landing distance, flaps 45, times 1.7. Given the winds we did not feel flaps 45 was appropriate so we ran the numbers flaps 22 times 1.7. The number we came up with was about 8,000 ft. and we had about 9,000 feet of available runway. We didn't feel comfortable with that number and decided, as a crew, we would request Runway XXL out of an abundance of caution. From this point we continued the flight and on the arrival extended the gear early, but the light did not extinguish. As previously briefed, we requested priority handling and asked for the longer runway.At some point on the approach, while deviating around a thunderstorm and lightning, we were read new winds which were still out of the south but at just 15 kts. We reran the numbers at flaps 45 times 1.7, per the QRH and had much better numbers, especially now that we had requested 15L. Throughout the whole flight, Name and I communicated with Dispatch, Maintenance, Passengers, our FA, and ATC to the greatest extent possible. Name requested from ATC to have the plane met by emergency vehicles and said that we would need a tow. I was a little confused because the QRH stated that we 'may' not have steering or reversers, but he told me we would not and that he had just done this in the sim the week prior. We continued that approach and had a safe landing, bringing the plane to a stop on the runway and emergency vehicles stated the aircraft seemed fine.Shortly after landing I inquired why we don't just try to taxi to the high speed using rudders or see if the steering worked. Name said he was sure it wouldn't work and was concerned about the possible of uncommanded swerving. We were towed to the gate and the passengers deplaned normally and no one was hurt. I believe we were in a high stress environment trying to accomplish a flight while also communicating with multiple agencies and dealing with bad weather. As the person reading the QRH I think I should've been more assertive with the fact that the QRH said 'may not have...'. I also feel I should've been more assertive once we were on the ground about attempting to taxi, in order to clear the runway. I also think Name may have had some training biases due to a recent similar training event in the sim. Later discussion made me realize that he thought we would have no brakes and no steering, where I was definitely under the impression it was just a possibility of no reversers and no steering. In the end we worked well as a crew, but there were some lapses in communication, but the overall outcome was a safe landing where no one was hurt.
ASRSN:1917229.s: The flight crew experienced an Air/Ground EICAS message during climbout from OKC, potentially indicating lost steering and thrust reversers. Despite communication lapses regarding the QRH's "may" language and training biases, they requested priority handling, landed safely on a longer runway, and were towed to the gate with no injuries.

ASRSN:1917239.n: Enroute we had an ECAM Caution Message of Landing Gear Control Interface Unit (LG LGCIU) 1 Fault message. After running the checklists and letting Maintenance Control know we elected to do a precautionary landing in the abundance of caution for any more landing gear issues. The landing was uneventful and we taxied to the gate on our own power where maintenance resolved the fault.
ASRSN:1917239.s: The crew received an LGCIU 1 fault ECAM caution enroute and elected a precautionary landing. The landing was uneventful, the aircraft taxied to the gate, and maintenance resolved the fault.

ASRSN:1917249.n: Had LE Flap extend after takeoff. Ran checklists and diverted to ZZZ.
ASRSN:1917249.s: The pilot reported left flap extension after takeoff. Following checklist execution, the aircraft was diverted to ZZZ.

ASRSN:1917278.n: On a ferry flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 we experienced a rapid decompression at FL 400. Both me and my First Officer noticed a pop-sound that came from the rear cabin aircraft. We immediately then looked at the cabin pressurization gauges and seen a rise in cabin altitude and rate of climb. I instructed my First Officer to don his oxygen mask and then I proceeded to don my mask. Also immediately after putting on my mask, the master warning light and the CABIN ALT Annunciator Light illuminated. My First Officer immediately requested a [priority] descent. We performed our required memory items and ran the appropriate checklist. We requested priority handling as a precaution and made a normal landing at ZZZ2.
ASRSN:1917278.s: During a ferry flight at FL 400, the Captain and First Officer experienced a rapid decompression caused by a pop sound from the rear cabin. They donned oxygen masks, requested a priority descent, and executed checklists before making a normal landing at ZZZ2.

ASRSN:1917283.n: We leveled off at 28,000 feet. I was listening to the MYR ATIS at the time, but was aware of ATC making altitude inquiries to an opposite direction Aircraft X. ATC was attempting to verify that Aircraft X was level at 27000 and that his altimeter was set to 29.92. The aircraft verified that he was at 27,000 and his altimeter was 29.92. However, he kept climbing. This began at a distance of 10 miles. Aircraft X continued to climb and we received an RA caution message. At this time, I paid sole attention to the TCAS alert and ATC. Suddenly, we received a TCAS warning with instructions to climb. The TCAS climb rate required as 2,200 feet per minute at 28,000 feet. We immediately complied with TCAS and I saw that we went over the top of Aircraft X just 300 feet below. Had we not immediately complied with the TCAS, it is likely that a mid air collision would have occurred. After the event was over, we asked ATC for information about the aircraft we just went over. They gave us a Center number to call, and we called it when safely on the ground. From the call, we learned the aircraft type, tail number, and that we had a closure rate of over 900 knots. We never saw Aircraft X as we were in IMC through the entire event.
ASRSN:1917283.s: The crew at 28,000 feet received a TCAS climb warning after Aircraft X continued climbing despite verifying 27,000 feet. They immediately complied with the 2,200 feet per minute climb instruction, passing 300 feet above Aircraft X in IMC, avoiding a likely mid-air collision.

ASRSN:1917293.n: On the ground just prior to push after flight deck pre-flight. The first officer got into his seat and the fire extinguisher fell off its mount. Onto flight deck floor. We put it back on mount but latch would not secure very tight, but held the extinguisher. During the after takeoff flow and checklist we found the gear lights disagreed and gear did not retract. 3 red and 3 green. Overhead lights all green. Ran QRH for gear handle in off position which determined gear down and locked. At the time we were 20,000 lbs. overweight. Asked for holding to burn fuel below max landing weight approx. 2.0 hours. Passenger and Flight Attendant briefed and checks completed. During communication with Dispatch was told to check manual gear extension door that was not in our QRH FLOW FOR GEAR IN OFF POSITION. Door was unlatched due to fire extinguisher falling on it. We did not see it or catch it due to IMC terrain and high work load. We then got gear to operate normally after latching door closed. At that time we had burned too much fuel to continue to ZZZ1. Burned fuel down landed uneventfully under max weight. Fire extinguisher latch and manual gear ext door was written up and put in logbook. Prior to push back, the First Officer's chair was moved forward and fire extinguisher fell on ground due to loose latch. Fire extinguisher was reinstalled to mount. After non-eventful taxi, First Officer took off in IMC in an area of high terrain and at night. It was discovered during the after takeoff checklist that the gear failed to retract (all lights illuminated). We [requested priority handling] and went to holding to run checklists and trouble shoot the issue. After running the checklist and contacting Dispatch we were advised to check the manual gear door. The manual gear door was not latched and suspected to have been unlatched by the fire extinguisher falling on it prior to takeoff. After the manual gear door was closed the gear was able to be retracted. Due to fuel requirements we were no longer able to proceed to ZZZ1 and burned off fuel to land back at ZZZ below max landing weight. Uneventful landing and taxi back to gate.
ASRSN:1917293.s: Prior to pushback, a loose fire extinguisher latch caused the unit to fall and unlatch the manual gear extension door. This prevented gear retraction after takeoff in IMC, requiring a fuel burn to land safely at the departure airport after the door was manually secured.

ASRSN:1917294.n: On VFR arrival to Runway XXC in ZZZ1, the flaps stopped between 15 and 25 degrees symmetrically. The anomaly was not noticed until the landing checklist was read at approximately 1,500 ft. There was no unusual roll or pitch as I was hand flying the aircraft at this point. After a brief discussion between the First Officer (FO) and I, we elected to use flaps 15 speed (only a few knots faster due to a very light landing weight) and continue the landing. Runway was dry and one of the longer runways in North America. Due to the last minute decision to continue late into the approach, no emergency was declared to ATC. We had to inhibit the flap inhibit when it sounded due to the flaps 15 landing. Landed uneventfully, wrote the flap anomaly up, and contacted Maintenance. After a de-brief at the gate, we decided that we made the correct decision under the circumstances.
ASRSN:1917294.s: During a VFR arrival to Runway XXC, flaps stopped symmetrically between 15 and 25 degrees, noticed at 1,500 ft.
